title: Tell the patient the absolute risk
lead: Counsel with the absolute risk reduction. A relative reduction of half can be one event in a thousand.
lines: Number needed to treat is 1 divided by that absolute difference.
A confidence interval that includes no difference is not a reason to change practice by itself.
A surrogate marker moving is not the same as a heart attack being prevented.
Screening recommendations are based on absolute benefits and harms. Relative reductions without the baseline risk mislead.
miss: Telling a patient a drug cuts risk in half without saying half of what.

source.name: USPSTF. Breast cancer screening.
source.says: Screening recommendations are based on absolute benefits and harms. Relative reductions without the baseline risk mislead, which is the recommendation in USPSTF. Breast cancer screening.

title: Stop lung screening 15 years after the last cigarette
lead: Stop annual lung-cancer screening when the patient has not smoked for 15 years, turns 81, or develops a condition that limits the benefit.
lines: Annual low-dose CT for ages 50–80 with at least 20 pack-years, current smoker or quit within 15 years.
A shared decision, including false positives, comes before the first scan.
Hemoptysis or a persistent new cough is a diagnostic CT, not a screening order.
miss: Continuing yearly scans in an 84-year-old who quit 20 years ago.

source.name: USPSTF. Lung cancer screening.
source.says: Screening should be discontinued once a person has not smoked for 15 years or develops a health problem that substantially limits life expectancy or the ability or willingness to have curative lung surgery.

title: Colon screening starts at 45 for average risk
lead: Average-risk colorectal screening starts at 45 and continues through 75. A first-degree relative with an early cancer starts earlier.
lines: Average-risk screening begins at 45. A positive stool-based test is followed by colonoscopy.
A positive stool test is a colonoscopy, not another card. Ages 76–85 are selective.
A first-degree relative with colorectal cancer before 60 starts earlier than 45, often 10 years before that diagnosis.
Iron deficiency in an older adult is a diagnostic colonoscopy, not a screening interval.
miss: Repeating a stool test after a positive one, instead of scoping.

source.name: USPSTF. Colorectal cancer screening.
source.says: Average-risk screening begins at 45. A positive stool-based test is followed by colonoscopy, which is the recommendation in USPSTF. Colorectal cancer screening.

title: Mammography is every other year from 40 through 74
lead: The USPSTF recommends mammography every other year from age 40 through 74. It does not recommend supplemental ultrasound for dense breasts as a proven add-on.
lines: Age 75 and older is an I statement. Decide with the patient.
A palpable mass is a diagnostic workup, not a screening interval.
A family history of a BRCA-associated cancer is a different, earlier plan.
Breast: biennial mammography ages 40 through 74. Colorectal: start at 45 through 75, and a positive stool test is a colonoscopy.
miss: Telling a 42-year-old to wait until 50 because that used to be the start.
diagramAlt: Mammography every other year from 40 to 74. Colon screening from 45. Lung screening is annual low-dose CT from 50 to 80 after 20 pack-years.

source.name: USPSTF. Breast cancer screening.
source.says: Biennial mammography from 40 through 74 is the recommendation. Supplemental imaging for density is not endorsed.

title: Cervical screening does not start before 21
lead: Cervical screening starts at 21. Ages 21 to 29 are cytology every 3 years. Ages 30 to 65 may use cytology every 3 years or high-risk HPV testing every 5.
lines: A vaccinated patient is still screened.
Yearly Pap smears are not the recommendation.
Bleeding after sex is a symptom and is examined now.
Types 16 and 18 cause most cervical cancers. Screening starts at 21, not at coitarche.
Ages 21–29: cytology every 3 years, not HPV testing alone. Ages 30–65: cytology every 3 years, HPV every 5, or cotesting every 5. Stop at 65 only if prior tests were adequate.
miss: Starting Pap smears at the first pelvic exam of a 16-year-old.

source.name: USPSTF. Cervical cancer screening.
source.says: Screening begins at 21. Intervals are every 3 years with cytology alone in younger women, with HPV options after 30.

title: Bone-density screening starts at 65 for women
lead: Women 65 and older are screened for osteoporosis with a bone-density test. A younger postmenopausal woman is screened only when her fracture risk matches that of a 65-year-old.
lines: DEXA is the test. A heel ultrasound is not the screening study.
A fragility fracture is already disease. It is treated, not filed as a normal screening interval.
Routine screening of men is not the task-force recommendation.
A normal result is not a yearly order. The repeat interval is individualized.
miss: Ordering a DEXA for every woman at 50, or skipping it at 65 because she has no back pain.

source.name: USPSTF. Osteoporosis to prevent fractures: screening.
source.says: Screen women 65 and older for osteoporosis with bone measurement testing, and screen younger postmenopausal women who are at increased risk.

title: Aspirin prevents preeclampsia only in the patients at high risk
lead: Low-dose aspirin after 12 weeks prevents preeclampsia in patients with a high-risk condition. It does not treat a pressure of 170.
lines: Prior preeclampsia, multifetal pregnancy, chronic hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, and autoimmune disease are the high-risk list.
The dose used in the recommendation is 81 mg.
Severe-range pressures are treated with antihypertensives and magnesium, not with aspirin.
miss: Starting aspirin at 34 weeks as the treatment of severe hypertension.

source.name: USPSTF. Aspirin Use to Prevent Preeclampsia.
source.says: Low-dose aspirin after 12 weeks is for prevention in high-risk patients. It is not the treatment of severe-range blood pressure, which is the recommendation in USPSTF. Aspirin Use to Prevent Preeclampsia.

title: The four abilities, for this decision
lead: Capacity is the ability to decide this question today: to understand, appreciate, reason, and say a choice.
lines: The four abilities are understanding the facts, appreciating what they mean, reasoning, and stating a choice.
The judgment is for this decision today. Refusing surgery does not cancel the ability to accept an antibiotic.
Fever, sodium, and sedatives can change the result. Recheck rather than stamp the chart.
Competence is the court's finding. Capacity is the clinician's judgment for this choice.
miss: Calling a patient incapacitated only because they refused the recommended operation.
diagramAlt: Capacity for this decision. Understand the facts Appreciate what they mean for you Reason, and say a stable choice

source.name: Appelbaum. Assessment of patients' competence to consent to treatment.
source.says: Capacity to consent requires understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and a choice, and the assessment is specific to the decision.

title: Tell the patient about the error
lead: A harmful error is disclosed to the patient: what happened, what it means, and what will be done next.
lines: Do not alter the record. Add a dated note.
An apology for the event is not a guess about legal fault.
Hiding the error, or telling only the family and not the patient who can hear it, fails the duty.
miss: Writing a vague note and hoping the next team explains it.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 8.6, Promoting Patient Safety.
source.says: AMA Opinion 8.6: disclose a medical error, explain the potential harm, and do not let concern about liability affect that honesty.

title: The surrogate uses the patient's standard
lead: A surrogate's job is substituted judgment: what this patient would have chosen. Best interest is the fallback when that is unknown.
lines: The family's preference, the oldest child's preference, and the team's preference are not the standard.
A written directive and prior statements outrank a surrogate's new opinion.
If no one knows what the patient would have wanted, choose what serves the patient's interests.
A directive that addresses this decision outranks a surrogate who now wants something else.
Surrogates decide according to the patient's previously expressed preferences, and according to the patient's best interest when preferences are unknown.
miss: Doing what the loudest relative demands because they are present.
diagramAlt: Who decides. Written directive that fits this choice wins Else substituted judgment Else best interest

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Decisions for Adult Patients Who Lack Capacity.
source.says: Surrogates decide according to the patient's previously expressed preferences, and according to the patient's best interest when preferences are unknown, which is the recommendation in AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Decisions for Adult Patients Who Lack Capacity.

title: A capacitated refusal stands
lead: A patient with capacity may refuse treatment, including treatment that would save their life.
lines: Confirm the four abilities for this decision, and confirm they heard the consequence.
Document the refusal and the reasons. Offer to revisit it.
A relative cannot overrule that refusal.
Understand, appreciate, reason, and state a choice, for this decision today. A refusal that meets those four is an order.
Disagreement with the team is not incapacity. Reassess when sodium, oxygen, or a sedative has changed. Competence is the court's word.
miss: Sedating a refusing patient, or asking the family to sign, because the team is sure the patient is wrong.
diagramAlt: Capacity for this decision. Understand the facts Appreciate what they mean for you Reason, and say a stable choice

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Decisions for adult patients who lack capacity.
source.says: When a patient lacks capacity, the surrogate decides by substituted judgment, then by best interest. A written directive that addresses the decision outranks a conflicting surrogate.

title: Consent is interpreted, not translated by the child
lead: A professional interpreter is used for consent when you and the patient do not share a language. A child or a family member is not the interpreter.
lines: Speak to the patient, not to the interpreter.
Document the interpreter's identity.
Informed consent requires disclosure a reasonable patient would want, the patient's understanding, and a voluntary decision. The clinician performing the procedure is responsible for that disclosure.
miss: Asking a 10-year-old to explain a surgery to a parent.

source.name: 45 CFR 92.201. Meaningful access for people with limited English proficiency.
source.says: A qualified interpreter must be offered. A minor child must not interpret, except briefly during an emergency while a qualified interpreter is found.

title: Emergency care proceeds when no one can consent
lead: If a patient cannot consent and no surrogate can be reached in time, emergency treatment that a reasonable person would want proceeds.
lines: This is implied consent for the emergency, not a blank check for elective procedures.
Document why you could not wait.
Informed consent requires disclosure a reasonable patient would want, the patient's understanding, and a voluntary decision. The clinician performing the procedure is responsible for that disclosure.
That note covers the emergency only. An elective addition waits. Keep looking for the surrogate.
miss: Withholding a life-saving procedure overnight because the family phone went to voicemail.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Informed consent.
source.says: Informed consent requires disclosure a reasonable patient would want, the patient's understanding, and a voluntary decision. The clinician performing the procedure is responsible for that disclosure, which is the recommendation in AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Informed consent.

title: A do-not-resuscitate order is not a do-not-treat order
lead: A do-not-resuscitate order means you do not attempt resuscitation if the heart stops. Antibiotics, surgery, and comfort care are separate decisions.
lines: Ask what the order was meant to cover.
A patient can want surgery and refuse resuscitation.
Do not withhold pain medicine because a DNR is on the chart.
A do-not-attempt-resuscitation order limits resuscitation. It does not by itself stop other treatments the patient still wants.
Write each limit. Comfort medication is ordered even when resuscitation is not.
miss: Cancelling the antibiotics because the chart says DNR.
diagramAlt: What DNR does not stop. No chest compressions if the heart stops Antibiotics, surgery, and opioids are separate Write each limit. Do not guess

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 5.4, orders not to attempt resuscitation.
source.says: A do-not-attempt-resuscitation order limits resuscitation. It does not by itself stop other treatments the patient still wants, which is the recommendation in AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 5.4, orders not to attempt resuscitation.

title: Withdrawing a ventilator is ethically the same as not starting it
lead: Stopping a treatment that is no longer wanted or no longer helps is ethically the same as never having started it.
lines: The goal is the patient's goal, not the team's discomfort.
Medicines for air hunger are given. The intent is comfort.
A slow wean that prolongs suffering to make the team feel better is not kinder.
Order an opioid for air hunger before the ventilator is withdrawn. The dose is the dose that relieves the symptom.
A dose chosen to relieve symptoms is not an order to end life. Withdrawing a treatment and never having started it are the same decision when the treatment no longer serves the patient's goal.
miss: Refusing to stop a ventilator the patient never wanted because stopping feels like killing.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 5.3, withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment.
source.says: Withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining treatment are ethically the same when the treatment no longer serves the patient's goals. Symptom relief continues.

title: A capable patient may refuse blood
lead: A capable adult may refuse blood, including when refusal may be fatal. You explain the consequence and you honor the refusal.
lines: Make sure the refusal is for this surgery and this risk.
A surrogate does not get to impose a refusal the patient never made, or to overturn one the patient did.
Children are treated with blood when it is life-saving even if a parent refuses.
Understand, appreciate, reason, and state a choice, for this decision today. A refusal that meets those four is an order.
miss: Transfusing a clearly refusing capable adult because the hemoglobin is 5.
diagramAlt: Capacity for this decision. Understand the facts Appreciate what they mean for you Reason, and say a stable choice

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Decisions for adult patients who lack capacity.
source.says: When a patient lacks capacity, the surrogate decides by substituted judgment, then by best interest. A written directive that addresses the decision outranks a conflicting surrogate.

title: Parents cannot refuse emergency care that saves a child
lead: Parents decide for a child except when refusal would cause death or serious harm. Then you treat and you involve the protective system.
lines: Elective care is different from a life-saving transfusion or an emergency surgery.
Suspected abuse or neglect is reported. A request to keep it private does not cancel the duty.
Explain once, then treat. Elective care is a different rule: a parent can decline a non-urgent procedure.
miss: Watching a child deteriorate because a parent declined an emergency operation.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 8.10, preventing, identifying, and treating violence and abuse.
source.says: Suspected abuse or neglect is reported. A request to keep it private does not cancel the duty, which is the recommendation in AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 8.10, preventing, identifying, and treating violence and abuse.

title: A pregnant patient with capacity decides, including a refusal of cesarean
lead: A capable pregnant patient decides about cesarean delivery. The fetus does not give a separate veto that lets you operate against her refusal.
lines: Explain the fetal risk in plain words.
Coercion and a court order are not the routine path.
A capable pregnant patient can refuse a cesarean, including when the fetal tracing is concerning. Document the risk you explained and do not write an order to proceed.
Continue to offer care. Fetal benefit does not erase that refusal.
miss: Taking a refusing patient to the operating room because the tracing is bad.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 1.1.3, Patient Rights.
source.says: AMA Opinion 1.1.3: a patient with decision-making capacity may accept or refuse any recommended medical intervention.

title: Sterilization consent is not obtained during labor
lead: Consent for sterilization is obtained before labor, when the patient can deliberate. A signature between contractions is not adequate consent.
lines: Pain, fear, and a power imbalance make labor the wrong moment.
A prior wish is revisited before the procedure, not assumed.
Document the earlier conversation.
A prior antenatal consent is confirmed on the day. It is not assumed. The cesarean still needs its own current consent.
miss: Adding a tubal ligation to a cesarean because the patient nodded during a contraction.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 2.1.1, Informed Consent.
source.says: AMA Opinion 2.1.1 requires an independent, voluntary decision after the patient understands the treatment and its alternatives.

title: The person doing the procedure obtains the consent
lead: Consent for a procedure is obtained by a clinician who understands the procedure and will participate. A student who has never done it does not obtain that consent alone.
lines: The patient is told who will be present and what a student will do.
A form signed for a different operation does not cover this one.
Questions are answered before the sedative is given.
Informed consent requires disclosure a reasonable patient would want, the patient's understanding, and a voluntary decision. The clinician performing the procedure is responsible for that disclosure.
miss: Sending a student who cannot explain the risks to get the signature.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Informed consent.
source.says: Informed consent requires disclosure a reasonable patient would want, the patient's understanding, and a voluntary decision. The clinician performing the procedure is responsible for that disclosure, which is the recommendation in AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Informed consent.

title: A sensitive exam uses a chaperone
lead: A breast, pelvic, or genital exam is done with a chaperone offered and, in many settings, present. The patient's comfort is part of consent.
lines: Explain each step before you do it.
A chaperone protects the patient and the clinician.
Stop if consent is withdrawn. An offer that was never made is not a decline.
miss: Proceeding with a pelvic exam after the patient asked you to stop.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 1.2.4, Use of Chaperones.
source.says: AMA Opinion 1.2.4: always honor a patient's request for a chaperone, and use an authorized member of the health care team.

title: Pain medicine at the end of life is not euthanasia
lead: Opioids given to treat pain or air hunger, even if they might hasten death, are not euthanasia when the intent is relief.
lines: Do not withhold morphine from a dying patient because of that confusion.
An opioid dose titrated to pain or air hunger is symptom treatment. The intent is relief, and the dose stops when the symptom stops.
A dose chosen to end life is a different act and is not what this order is. Write the symptom you are treating.
miss: Leaving a dying patient in pain to avoid a theoretical hastening of death.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 5.6, Sedation to Unconsciousness in End-of-Life Care.
source.says: AMA Opinion 5.6: the duty to relieve pain is central, and sedation to unconsciousness must never be used to intentionally cause a patient's death.

title: An impaired colleague is your problem
lead: If a colleague's impairment puts patients at risk, you act. Silence is not loyalty.
lines: Report through the system your institution requires.
A rumor is not the same as an observed impairment. Act on what you know.
Remove the colleague from patients immediately if the impairment is happening now. The report does not wait until the end of the shift.
Review patients already seen. A hallway announcement is not the reporting channel.
miss: Letting an intoxicated colleague finish the shift because confronting them is awkward.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 9.3.2, Responsibilities to Colleagues with Impairment.
source.says: Intervene when a colleague cannot practice safely, so the colleague is no longer endangering patients, and see that the person gets evaluation and care.

title: Do not alter the record
lead: A late correction is added, dated, and signed. The original note is not deleted or rewritten after a bad outcome.
lines: Changing a note to hide an error is a second harm.
The disclosure to the patient and the note tell the same story.
A correction after a complication is an addendum with the time you learned the fact. The original note stays.
miss: Editing yesterday's note after the complication to make the plan look safer.

source.name: AMA Principles of Medical Ethics, Principle II.
source.says: AMA Principle II: a physician shall be honest in all professional interactions.

title: Research consent is not clinical consent
lead: Enrolling a patient in research requires a research consent that explains the study, the alternatives, and the right to leave. The treatment consent does not cover it.
lines: The patient can decline the study and still receive care.
A power imbalance means you do not pressure.
The consent names what is experimental.
The surgical consent does not enroll the patient. The person obtaining research consent can explain the protocol.
miss: Adding a research biopsy because the patient already signed the surgery consent.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 7.1.2, Informed Consent in Research.
source.says: No one may be used in research against their will. Voluntary informed consent is required before a person is enrolled in a research protocol.

title: A placebo given as if it were treatment is a deception
lead: Giving a placebo while telling the patient it is an active drug is a deception. It is not a clever therapeutic trial.
lines: If a placebo is studied, the consent says so.
Symptoms still get a real evaluation.
Trust, once broken, ruins the next true recommendation.
Labeling a sugar capsule as an active analgesic is deception. It is not a therapeutic trial.
miss: Prescribing a sugar pill for pain and calling it a strong analgesic.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 2.1.4, use of placebo in clinical practice.
source.says: Giving a placebo while telling the patient it is an active drug is a deception. It is not a therapeutic trial.

title: Suspected child abuse is reported without a parent's permission
lead: Suspected child abuse is reported. You do not need the parent's permission, and you do not need proof.
lines: Treat the injury.
The report is to the agency the law names.
A parent who asks you not to report is the reason the duty does not sit with the parent.
Report on suspicion before discharge. A parent's request to keep it private is not a hold. Proof is not the threshold.
Photograph patterned injuries and treat them. Do not discharge to the suspected person while you think about reporting tomorrow.
miss: Agreeing to keep a suspicious fracture between you and the family.
diagramAlt: Report abuse. Suspicion is enough. Proof is not Parent or caregiver cannot veto it Treat the injury and make the report

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 8.10, preventing, identifying, and treating violence and abuse.
source.says: Suspected abuse or neglect is reported. A request to keep it private does not cancel the duty.

title: Organ donation is asked separately from the decision to stop support
lead: The treating team does not couple the request for organs to the moment they recommend stopping support. A designated requester has that conversation.
lines: The decision to stop is the patient's or the surrogate's, made on its own merits.
A conflict of interest is avoided by separating the roles.
The patient who wanted to donate still can. The timing of the ask is what changes.
The decision to stop support is made on its own merits. A designated requester, not the treating team, asks about donation.
miss: Saying you will stop the ventilator if the family agrees to donation.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 6.1.1, organ donation and transplantation.
source.says: The decision to stop support is separate from the request for organ donation, which is made by a designated requester.

title: A POLST is an order. An advance directive is a statement
lead: A POLST or similar portable order tells emergency clinicians what to do tonight. An advance directive tells a surrogate what the patient would have wanted.
lines: They are not interchangeable.
A POLST is a medical order emergency clinicians can follow. An advance directive guides a surrogate and does not travel in an ambulance unless a copy is present.
Reconcile conflicting orders before discharge. A capable patient can void either.
miss: Ignoring a POLST that says do not intubate because an old advance directive was vague.
diagramAlt: POLST versus advance directive. POLST is an order paramedics can follow A directive guides the surrogate A form in a safe does not travel

source.name: National POLST. What a POLST form is.
source.says: A POLST form is a portable medical order. For someone who is healthy, an advance directive, not a POLST form, is the planning tool.

title: Against-medical-advice discharge still gets an explanation
lead: A capable patient may leave against advice. You explain the risk, treat what you still can, and document. You do not punish the patient by withholding a prescription they need for a safe exit.
lines: Confirm capacity for this decision.
Offer to treat the dangerous problem before they go.
A signature is not required for you to have had the conversation, and refusal to sign is documented.
A capable patient may leave. Offer the antibiotic or insulin that makes leaving safer. Do not withhold it as a punishment.
miss: Refusing to give a needed antibiotic because the patient is leaving against advice.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 1.1.3, Patient Rights.
source.says: A patient with decision-making capacity may refuse recommended care, and has a right to discuss the risks of forgoing treatment.

title: You do not offer a treatment that cannot work
lead: You do not offer a menu of interventions that cannot achieve the patient's goal. Futility is explained, and comfort is offered.
lines: The word is used carefully. A treatment that is unlikely is not the same as one that cannot work.
A second opinion is reasonable. A false hope is not.
The family is not asked to choose among useless options.
Do not offer an intervention that cannot achieve a physiologic goal, such as compressions that cannot restore a circulation.
miss: Asking a family whether they want chest compressions that cannot restore a dead circulation, as if it were a real choice.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 5.5, Medically Ineffective Interventions.
source.says: Physicians are not required to offer or to provide interventions that, in their best medical judgment, cannot reasonably be expected to yield the intended clinical benefit or achieve agreed-on goals for care.

title: A scarce bed follows a rule you could defend in public
lead: When two patients need one bed or one drug, the rule is clinical and stated in advance. Friendship, fame, and anger do not move the list.
lines: Write the rule before you know the names: acuity, and whether the bed changes the outcome.
A stable patient does not outrank a patient in shock because a colleague called.
If acuity is truly equal, use a tie-break stated in advance. Record that clinical reason in the chart.
The same rule is used on the next shift. Changing it after you see the names is the failure.
miss: Giving the last ICU bed to a colleague's relative who is less sick.

source.name: AMA Code of Medical Ethics. Opinion 11.1.3, Allocating Limited Health Care Resources.
source.says: AMA Opinion 11.1.3: a scarce bed is allocated by a policy based on medical need, including urgency and the likelihood and duration of benefit.
